text:
This bar chart compares ImageNet top-1 accuracy across five models.

The horizontal axis is labeled Model. The vertical axis is labeled Top-1 accuracy, in percent, and runs from 70 to 88 rather than starting at zero. It is not logarithmic.

From left to right, the models are ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ConvNeXt-T, Swin-T, and Ours.

Their accuracies are 76.1, 81.8, 82.1, 81.3, and 84.6 percent, respectively.

Ours has the highest accuracy, while ResNet-50 has the lowest. The other three models cluster between 81.3 and 82.1 percent.

This is a heat map titled “Layer 6, head 3 attention,” showing attention values between query and key tokens.

The horizontal axis is labeled “Key token,” and the vertical axis is labeled “Query token.” Both list the same seven tokens in order: capitalized “The,” “cat,” “sat,” “on,” lowercase “the,” “mat,” and a period. The color scale runs from 0 to 1, with dark purple near zero and yellow at 1.

The main diagonal values, in token order, are about 1.0, 0.91, 0.82, 0.84, 0.74, 0.38, and 0.63. The largest off-diagonal value is about 0.47, for the query “mat” and the key “cat.” Other visible off-diagonal values are mostly below 0.15.

Attention is concentrated along the diagonal, where each query attends to the matching key. The “mat” query is the exception: it attends more strongly to “cat” than to itself. Cells above the diagonal are near zero.

This line chart shows validation loss during training for three methods.

The horizontal axis is training step, from 0 to 10,000 steps. The vertical axis is cross-entropy loss, with labeled ticks from 1.5 to 4.5; it does not start at zero. Both axes are linear.

The three series are Baseline in blue, plus LoRA in orange, and Full fine-tune in green.

All three start at about 4.5 loss. At 4,000 steps, Baseline is about 2.25, plus LoRA about 2.13, and Full fine-tune about 2.06. At 6,000 steps, they are about 2.15, 1.94, and 1.80, respectively. At 10,000 steps, they end at about 2.08, 1.85, and 1.63.

Loss drops steeply for all three methods early on, then declines more gradually. After roughly 4,000 steps, Full fine-tune has the lowest loss, plus LoRA is in the middle, and Baseline is highest. The Baseline line levels off near 2.1, while the other two continue to decline.

This grouped bar chart shows scores on three benchmarks for three model sizes.

The horizontal axis is labeled Benchmark and lists GLUE, SuperGLUE, and SQuAD F1. The vertical axis is labeled Score, with no units shown. It is linear and runs from 50 to 100, so it does not start at zero.

The model size groups are Small, shown in blue; Base, in orange; and Large, in green.

For GLUE, the scores are about 78 for Small, 84.3 for Base, and 88.8 for Large. For SuperGLUE, they are about 64.8, 71.1, and 79.2, respectively. For SQuAD F1, they are about 82.9, 88.4, and 91.

Scores rise with model size on every benchmark. SQuAD F1 has the highest scores for all three sizes, while SuperGLUE has the lowest. The overall maximum is about 91 for Large on SQuAD F1, and the minimum is about 64.8 for Small on SuperGLUE.

This is a confusion matrix heat map showing test-set true labels against predicted labels.

The horizontal axis is Predicted label, and the vertical axis is True label. Both are categorical, with no units or numerical ranges. Each lists cat, dog, bird, and car, in that order. The blue color scale has labeled ticks from 0 to 80, in steps of 20; darker blue indicates higher values.

Reading across each row in predicted-label order, the true cat row is 88, 9, 2, and 1. The dog row is 11, 84, 3, and 2. The bird row is 3, 4, 90, and 3. The car row is 0, 1, 2, and 97.

The largest values lie on the diagonal, where true and predicted labels match. Car has the highest diagonal value, 97, and dog the lowest, 84. The largest off-diagonal value is 11, for true dogs predicted as cats. The minimum is 0, for true cars predicted as cats.

This scatter plot shows MMLU scores against model parameter counts.

The horizontal axis is Parameters, in billions, spanning about 3 to 72 billion. The vertical axis is MMLU, in percent, spanning about 55 to 88 percent. Both axes are linear and neither starts at zero.

The legend identifies three families: Dense, shown as blue circles; MoE, as orange crosses; and Distilled, as green squares.

Dense points range from about 5.8 billion parameters and 56.7 percent to a high of about 65 billion and 86.9 percent. The rightmost Dense point is about 68 billion and 84.8 percent. MoE ranges from about 5.7 billion and 56.2 percent to about 66 billion and 86.9 percent. Distilled ranges from about 11 billion and 61 percent to a high of about 68 billion and 81.7 percent; its rightmost point is about 68.5 billion and 78.1 percent.

Scores generally rise with parameter count, though there is variation at similar sizes. MoE points are often above Dense and Distilled points, while Distilled points generally score lowest. At the high end, Dense and MoE reach nearly 87 percent, while Distilled remains below 82 percent.

This box plot shows the distribution of inference latency across four types of hardware.

The horizontal axis is labeled Hardware. The vertical axis is labeled Latency, in milliseconds, and is linear. It extends from slightly below zero to about 200 milliseconds, with labeled ticks from zero to 175.

The four groups are CPU, GPU, TPU, and Edge NPU.

For CPU, the median is about 116 milliseconds, the box extends from about 106 to 141, and the whiskers extend from about 68 to 190. For GPU, the median is about 16 milliseconds, the box spans about 14 to 20, and the whiskers span about 10 to 28, with an outlier at about 29. For TPU, the median is about 11 milliseconds, the box spans about 9 to 14, and the whiskers span about 7 to 20, with outliers around 22 and 24. For Edge NPU, the median is about 44 milliseconds, the box spans about 38 to 48, and the whiskers span about 24 to 62. Its high outliers are approximately 65, 69, 73, 76, and 87 milliseconds.

CPU has the highest latency and the widest spread. Edge NPU is next, while GPU and TPU are much lower, with TPU having the lowest median.

This split violin chart shows score distributions for three tasks, comparing performance with and without chain-of-thought prompting.

There is one panel. The horizontal axis is labeled Task and lists Math, Code, and Writing. The vertical axis is labeled Score, with no units shown. It is linear and runs from about 18 to 110, with labeled ticks from 20 to 100, so it does not start at zero.

Each violin is split into two groups: blue for Without CoT and orange for With CoT.

The middle horizontal marks are at about 55 without CoT and 74 with CoT for Math, about 55 and 64 for Code, and about 54 and 56 for Writing. The outer horizontal marks are roughly 48 and 62 without CoT and 67 and 79 with CoT for Math; 49 and 62 without and 58 and 70 with for Code; and 48 and 61 without and 48 and 64 with for Writing.

With CoT, the distributions shift noticeably higher for Math and Code, especially Math. The Writing distributions overlap much more, with their middle marks only about two points apart. Among the three tasks, Math with CoT has the highest middle mark.

This is an overlaid histogram with smooth curves showing the distributions of logit margins for two groups.

The horizontal axis is logit margin, ranging from about minus 3.5 to 5.1, so it does not start at zero. The vertical axis is count, ranging from zero to about 185. Both axes are linear.

The legend identifies the blue series as in-distribution and the orange series as out-of-distribution.

The in-distribution bars extend from about minus 3.1 to 3.4, with the tallest bar reaching 175 near minus 0.3. Its smooth curve peaks at about 158 near the same margin. The out-of-distribution bars extend from about 1.2 to 4.7, with the tallest bar reaching about 137 near 3.1. Its smooth curve peaks at about 135 near 3.1.

The in-distribution values are broadly spread around zero, while the out-of-distribution values form a narrower cluster around 3. The groups overlap mainly between margins of about 1.5 and 2.5, and their smooth curves cross near 1.9.

This scatter plot shows throughput generally increasing with compute, with a reported correlation of 0.94.

The horizontal axis is GPU hours, in thousands, ranging from slightly below zero to just above 10. The vertical axis is tokens per second, in thousands, ranging from about 1 to 27; it does not start at zero. Both axes are linear.

There is no legend. Blue dots show individual observations, and a blue line with a pale shaded band shows the overall trend.

The lowest dot is at about 0.6 thousand GPU hours and 2.5 thousand tokens per second. The highest is at about 8.6 thousand GPU hours and 26 thousand tokens per second. The trend line rises from about 5 thousand tokens per second at zero GPU hours to about 25 thousand at 10 thousand GPU hours.

The relationship is strongly positive, though there is some scatter. Notable points below the trend include one at about 6.3 thousand GPU hours and 12.7 thousand tokens per second. A point at about 0.7 thousand GPU hours and 12 thousand tokens per second lies well above the trend.

This is a line chart showing how test error changes with dataset size for three optimizers.

The horizontal axis is dataset size in tokens, on a logarithmic scale, with labeled ticks from one million to ten billion. The vertical axis is error, with no unit shown; it runs from about 0.75 to 3.15 and does not start at zero.

The legend identifies SGD in blue, Adam in orange, and Muon in green. Each line has circular markers and a narrow shaded band around it.

At one million tokens, all three errors are about 3. At 100 million tokens, SGD is about 1.99, Adam 1.89, and Muon 1.70. At one billion tokens, they are about 1.63, 1.45, and 1.26, respectively. At ten billion tokens, their final values are about 1.34 for SGD, 1.15 for Adam, and 0.91 for Muon.

Error decreases throughout for all three optimizers. Muon is generally lowest, Adam is in the middle, and SGD is highest; the lines separate more as dataset size increases.

This figure contains two line charts showing accuracy over training epochs and final validation accuracy across learning rates.

The left panel, Accuracy, plots epoch from 0 to 30 against accuracy, with labeled values from 0.3 to 1.0; the accuracy axis does not start at zero. The right panel, Learning-rate sweep, plots learning rate from 0.0001 to 0.01 on a logarithmic axis against final validation accuracy, with labeled values from 0.65 to 0.90; that accuracy axis also does not start at zero. Accuracy and learning rate have no units shown.

The left panel has blue Train and orange Validation lines, plus a dashed vertical marker at epoch 12. The right panel has one blue line with square markers and no legend.

Both left-panel lines start at about 0.26 at epoch 1 and reach about 0.92 at epoch 12. Training accuracy continues rising to about 1.00 at epoch 30. Validation accuracy peaks at about 0.95 around epoch 17, then falls to about 0.87 at epoch 30.

In the right panel, final validation accuracy is 0.81 at learning rate 0.0001, 0.86 at about 0.0003, 0.89 at 0.001, 0.84 at about 0.003, and 0.62 at 0.01.

The training and validation curves initially overlap, then diverge as validation accuracy declines. In the sweep, accuracy peaks at 0.001 and drops sharply at the highest learning rate.

This is a three-panel line chart showing accuracy over training epochs for three datasets, with and without augmentation.

Each panel has a horizontal axis labeled Epoch, with ticks from 0 to 100, and a vertical axis labeled Accuracy, with ticks from 0 to 0.8. The plotted accuracy range extends slightly below zero to about 1. Both axes are linear.

From left to right, the panels are CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet. In each panel, the blue line is None and the orange line is RandAugment.

All lines start at approximately zero. For CIFAR-10, at epoch 50, accuracy is about 0.83 without augmentation and 0.88 with RandAugment. At epoch 100, the values are about 0.91 and 0.94. RandAugment peaks at about 0.95 around epoch 90.

For CIFAR-100, the values at epoch 50 are about 0.64 and 0.69, rising to about 0.69 and 0.75 at epoch 100.

For Tiny-ImageNet, the values at epoch 50 are about 0.50 and 0.55, rising to about 0.55 and 0.60 at epoch 100.

Accuracy rises quickly at first and then levels off in all three panels. RandAugment stays above no augmentation after the start. CIFAR-10 has the highest accuracy, followed by CIFAR-100, then Tiny-ImageNet.

This is an error-bar chart showing mean BLEU scores for four model variants, with standard deviations over five seeds.

There is one panel. The horizontal axis, labeled Variant, lists the four variants. The vertical axis, labeled BLEU, runs from about 55.3 to 73.6, with labeled ticks from 57.5 to 72.5. It is linear and does not start at zero.

The groups are Full model, minus attention, minus residual, and minus norm.

The full model scores about 71.5, with an error range from 70.3 to 72.8. Minus attention scores about 65.3, ranging from 64.2 to 66.4. Minus residual scores about 56.6, ranging from 56.2 to 56.9. Minus norm scores about 66.6, ranging from 65.0 to 68.2.

The full model has the highest score. Minus norm ranks second, followed by minus attention, while minus residual is much lower than all the others.

This is a nine-panel scatterplot matrix titled “Feature pairs by species,” showing relationships and distributions for three flower measurements.

The columns, from left to right, show petal length, petal width, and sepal length on the horizontal axes. The rows show the same measurements, in the same order, on the vertical axes. The diagonal panels show distributions instead of scatterplots. The top row contains petal length’s distribution and its comparisons with petal width and sepal length; the middle row contains petal width’s comparisons and distribution; and the bottom row does the same for sepal length. Units are not specified. All measurement axes are linear and extend beyond the data rather than starting at zero. Across the panels, petal length spans roughly 0.3 to 6.6, petal width roughly minus 0.3 to 2.6, and sepal length roughly 3.6 to 7.9. The diagonal density scales are not labeled.

The groups are setosa-like in blue, versicolor-like in orange, and virginica-like in green.

The distribution peaks are about 1.5, 4.3, and 5.5 for petal length; about 0.3, 1.4, and 2.0 for petal width; and about 5.1, 5.9, and 6.5 for sepal length, in the same group order. The observed points range approximately from 1 to 6 in petal length, zero to 2.3 in petal width, and 4.3 to 7.3 in sepal length.

The groups form distinct clusters for petal measurements, with setosa-like smallest and virginica-like largest. Sepal lengths overlap more. Petal length and width rise together strongly.

This is a clustered heat map showing normalized task scores for five models across six tasks.

The horizontal axis lists tasks, and the vertical axis lists models; neither axis has units or a numerical range. The color scale runs from about 0 in dark blue to 1 in dark red, with ticks labeled 0.5 and 1. Dendrograms above and to the left show the clustering, without labeled distance scales.

From left to right, the tasks are Trans., Code, Math, Summ., QA, and NLI. From top to bottom, the models are M3, M4, M2, M1, and M5.

In task order, M3 scores about 0.73, 1.00, 0.82, 0.36, 0.01, and 0.01. M4 scores about 0.55, 0.84, 0.84, 0.52, 0.30, and 0.12. M2 scores about 0.11, 0.21, 0.22, 0.50, 0.78, and 0.37. M1 scores about 0.28, 0.08, 0.13, 0.84, 0.59, and 0.66. M5 scores about 0.19, 0.05, 0.15, 0.80, 0.68, and 0.78.

The highest score is M3 on Code, while its QA and NLI scores are near zero. M3 and M4 cluster together, as do M1 and M5. Code and Math cluster together, as do QA and NLI. M3 and M4 score relatively highly on Code and Math, whereas M1 and M5 score relatively highly on Summ., QA, and NLI.

This line chart shows the distribution of response lengths for two decoding methods.

The horizontal axis is labeled Tokens generated, with ticks from zero to 1,600; the plotted range extends slightly below zero. The vertical axis is labeled Proportion and runs from zero to one. Both axes are linear.

The legend identifies Greedy in blue and Speculative in orange.

Both curves start near zero tokens and a proportion of zero. At 100 tokens, Greedy is at about 0.16 and Speculative at about 0.5. At 200 tokens, they are at about 0.4 and 0.86, respectively. At 400 tokens, Greedy is at about 0.73 and Speculative is close to 1. Speculative reaches 1 at about 450 tokens. Greedy reaches about 0.92 at 600 tokens and approaches 1 between about 1,200 and 1,600 tokens.

The Speculative curve rises much more steeply and remains above the Greedy curve until both approach 1, showing that its responses are generally shorter.

This horizontal bar chart shows the number of papers in the survey by venue.

The horizontal axis is labeled “count” and runs from zero to about 430 papers, with labeled ticks every 50 up to 400. It is linear. The vertical axis is labeled “Venue.”

There is no legend. From top to bottom, the venues are NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, CVPR, and EMNLP.

The counts are about 411 for NeurIPS, 304 for ICML, 376 for ICLR, 157 for ACL, 288 for CVPR, and 132 for EMNLP.

NeurIPS has the most papers, followed by ICLR. ICML and CVPR are close together, while ACL and EMNLP have substantially fewer papers. EMNLP has the fewest.
